content: 1. Countries with a well-functioning national “Baby-friendly” hospital designation program should not view the updated implementation guidance as a reason to discontinue their successful programs. Instead, they should develop a plan to integrate the revised Ten Steps into their national Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative (BFHI) standards. A transition plan should outline when facilities are expected to comply with the updated standards and utilize the new tools. Facilities already designated or in the process of designation should be given adequate time to adapt their practices before the new standards become mandatory. 2. In the past, many countries used Picasso’s artwork, Maternity, for plaques or posters when designating facilities as “Baby-friendly.” However, WHO and UNICEF will no longer provide reproductions of this image. Countries using designation as an incentive for BFHI compliance will need to create their own imagery for this purpose. 3. Where “mother-friendly” criteria that extend beyond the Ten Steps have been incorporated into the designation criteria, these can remain unless there is a specific reason to update them. While maintaining a designation program, countries should also work on integrating the Ten Steps into national policies, quality improvement initiatives, and maternal and child health programs. 4. For countries without an active or successful BFHI program, it is recommended to focus on integrating and institutionalizing the Ten Steps using a quality-improvement approach at the facility level. This should be supported by a robust policy environment and mechanisms for monitoring and accountability. Staff and management at facilities previously designated as “Baby-friendly” should be informed of policy changes, updated standards, and the actions required to comply with these standards. 5. The revised Ten Steps to Successful Breastfeeding (2018) emphasize critical management procedures and key clinical practices. These include having a written breastfeeding policy communicated to all healthcare staff, training staff in necessary skills, informing pregnant women about breastfeeding benefits, and supporting mothers to initiate breastfeeding within the first hour after birth. 6. Facilities should ensure that mothers are shown how to breastfeed and maintain lactation, even if separated from their infants. Newborns should not be given food or drink other than breast milk unless medically indicated. Rooming-in practices should be encouraged, allowing mothers and infants to remain together 24 hours a day. 7. Mothers should be supported to recognize and respond to their infants’ feeding cues and encouraged to breastfeed on demand. The use of artificial teats, pacifiers, or feeding bottles should be discouraged unless medically necessary. If expressed breast milk or other feeds are required, alternative feeding methods such as cups or spoons are preferable. 8. Facilities should foster the establishment of breastfeeding support groups and refer mothers to these groups upon discharge. Community resources should be leveraged to provide ongoing breastfeeding support. 9. The responsibilities of national breastfeeding or BFHI coordinating bodies, as outlined in the guidance, apply regardless of whether a country operates a designation program. These responsibilities include integrating breastfeeding support into national health strategies and ensuring the sustainability of breastfeeding initiatives. 10. The revised BFHI guidance aligns with WHO recommendations and global strategies for protecting, promoting, and supporting breastfeeding in facilities providing maternity and newborn services. It emphasizes the importance of evidence-based practices and the integration of breastfeeding support into broader maternal and child health frameworks.
